Here's the lay of the land: body text currently renders in **Open Sans**, loaded as a webfont via Astro's font API (`astro.config.mjs`) and wired in as the `--font-sans` token (`src/styles/global.css:6`), which Tailwind's preflight applies to `<body>` by default. Headings stay on Literata (serif) and your name uses the handwriting font — those wouldn't be touched either way.

Your proposed stack is just the classic Apple/system-UI fallback chain (San Francisco on Apple devices → Helvetica Neue/Helvetica/Arial elsewhere). There isn't one unambiguous way to "add" it — where it goes in the stack changes the actual visible result:

**Plan A — Replace Open Sans entirely (recommended if you want the native/system look)**
- Set `--font-sans` to the system stack, drop the Open Sans entry from `astro.config.mjs` and its `<Font>` preload tag.
- Result: every visitor sees their OS's native UI font (San Francisco on Mac/iOS, Segoe UI-ish via fallback on Windows since it'd drop to Arial, Roboto-adjacent on Android via Arial). Zero webfont latency/FOUT, lighter page weight, feels like a native app. You lose the distinct "Open Sans" character as your brand voice for body copy.

**Plan B — System font first, Open Sans as fallback**
- `--font-sans: -apple-system, BlinkMacSystemFont, "Helvetica Neue", Helvetica, Arial, var(--font-open-sans), sans-serif;`
- Result: Mac/iOS Safari and Chrome-on-Mac users (where `-apple-system`/`BlinkMacSystemFont` resolve) never see Open Sans — the system keyword wins over the loaded webfont. Everyone else (Windows, Linux, Android) still gets Open Sans. Inconsistent look across platforms, and you'd still be paying to load/preload Open Sans for users who'll never see it.

**Plan C — Open Sans first, system stack as the fallback/safety net (standard practice)**
- `--font-sans: var(--font-open-sans), -apple-system, BlinkMacSystemFont, "Helvetica Neue", Helvetica, Arial, sans-serif;`
- Result: no visible change for anyone once Open Sans loads — it's just a better fallback than the generic `sans-serif` you'd otherwise end on (covers the instant before the webfont loads, and any failure case). Doesn't address your actual question of "is the system font nicer," since Open Sans still wins everywhere.

**Plan D — Leave it as is.**

Given you're asking "is this nicer," that's a look-and-feel call only you can make — A and B produce visibly different results depending on platform, so I don't want to guess which you're after.

What I actually know comes from this codebase and conversation: software engineer + social entrepreneur, into AI ethics/data sovereignty/a "post-extractive web", you work at Liva Healthcare, co-founded a few startups before, hobbies are photos/guitar/bouldering (currently commented out of the index), you've got a story-driven Copenhagen album, and a "digital garden" with seedling/budding/evergreen essays. That's the material I'm working from.

**On the looping trip-video idea:** I'd push back gently before building it. Two real snags:

1. Browsers block autoplay audio — a video "with simple music playing over and over" can't actually autoplay with sound unless it's muted, or the visitor clicks play first. So the idea as literally stated isn't buildable as a passive loop; it'd need to be muted-by-default (visual only) or opt-in.
2. It's in tension with the site you've already built. Everything here — the CLS-safe image pipeline, the story-driven albums instead of autoplay carousels, the "post-extractive web" line in your own description — reads as a deliberate stance against attention-grabbing, autoplaying media. A looping video-with-music on the homepage is the classic extractive-web pattern (autoplay, loop, hijack attention). It'd undercut the thing you're actually saying about yourself.

A muted, silent loop (no music) is a tamer version that avoids both problems — but even then it's a media-weight/motion-respecting tradeoff worth being deliberate about.

**Other directions that fit what's already here, roughly cheapest → most involved:**

- **A "now" strip** — a few plain lines near the top: current trip/location, what you're building, what you're reading or listening to. Pure text, zero media cost, extends the garden metaphor you already have (seedling/budding/evergreen) into "what's alive right now."

- **One still photo, not a video** — pull a single real shot from your own albums (you already have the ImageKit pipeline for this) as a quiet hero image behind the intro text. Static, fast, no motion/audio questions at all.
- **An opt-in audio clip** — a short guitar recording behind a play button near your handwriting signature. Intimate and unique, but the visitor chooses to hit play — no autoplay conflict.
- **Muted looping clip, your original idea, tamed** — one of your trip clips, silent, small, behind/above the intro text, with a tap-to-unmute control and respecting `prefers-reduced-motion` (pause for those who've asked for it).

Checked the raw HTML/CSS (it's a Framer site, but the technique itself is framework-agnostic). Here's exactly how it works:

**Structure:** behind the actual nav content there's a separate fixed container, same width as the viewport, ~108px tall (matching the header height), `z-index` *below* the nav links, `pointer-events: none` (so it's purely visual, doesn't block clicks). Inside it are **8 stacked, absolutely-positioned divs**, each `inset: 0` (same size, fully overlapping).

Each of the 8 divs has two things:
1. `backdrop-filter: blur(Npx)` where N doubles every layer: `0.078125px → 0.15625 → 0.3125 → 0.625 → 1.25 → 2.5 → 5 → 10px`.
2. `mask-image: linear-gradient(to bottom, transparent, black, black, transparent)` — but each layer's gradient stops are shifted down 12.5% from the last (layer 1 occupies the 0–37.5% band, layer 2 the 12.5–50% band, and so on, 8 layers × 12.5% = the full height).

The mask controls *where that layer's blur is visible*. Stacked together, this produces a smooth ramp — almost no blur at the very top, increasing continuously to a full 10px blur by the bottom of the bar — instead of the hard, flat edge you get from one `backdrop-filter: blur(10px)` over the whole header (which looks like a pane of glass was dropped in with a visible seam). This exact pattern is the standard "progressive/variable blur" trick for nav bars (same idea Apple uses natively in iOS/macOS toolbars).

**Why it's cheap:** zero JavaScript — no scroll listener recalculating anything. `backdrop-filter` is GPU-composited, and the masks are static gradients computed once. The browser just composites 8 pre-blurred, pre-masked layers; nothing reruns per frame on scroll.

That's a design magnitude question now, not a measurement one, so rather than guess a fourth number: which of these is closer to what you want?

2. **Keep the header's size, but compress the blur transition into a smaller top portion** of it (e.g. the top 40-50%), leaving the rest of the header crisp/unblurred — same header, shorter visible "fade."
3. **Keep the current span, just lower the max blur strength** (e.g. 10px → 4-5px) so it covers the same height but reads as lighter/subtler rather than shorter.

That pasted markup answers it — two things I had wrong:

1. **The gradient direction is `to top`, not `to bottom`.** I'd flipped which blur value went on which layer while keeping the gradient pointing down; the real site instead keeps blur values on their original layers and just flips the gradient axis. Those aren't equivalent.
2. **That's exactly why your "height looks smaller" question has a real answer:** with `to top`, layer 8 (the strongest, `10px` blur)'s mask only resolves inside the box between `87.5%` and `100%` — its `black 100%, black 112.5%` plateau is mostly *past* the top edge, clipped off. So the strongest blur never gets to hold a flat plateau at all — it only ever reaches full strength right at the very top pixel. The *visible*, strongly-blurred band ends up compressed into roughly the top 12% of the container, not spread across the whole thing. My version spread the strong blur across the top 37.5% instead — which is exactly why mine looked taller/heavier than the reference, even at the same container height.

Fixing both — reverting to the original blur-to-layer mapping and flipping the direction to `to top`:
